name: Reporting Under More Than One Standard
title: Reporting Under More Than One Standard
answer: Reporting under more than one standard means preparing financial statements or reconciliations under two or more accounting frameworks, such as IFRS and US GAAP, or local statutory rules and a group standard. It covers primary statements, notes, segment disclosures, and the reconciliation schedules that explain why profit, equity, or cash flow differ between frameworks. The work sits with group finance, technical accounting, and external reporting teams, and it often involves auditors and regulators in each jurisdiction. The scope is not just translation of numbers, because recognition, measurement, presentation, and disclosure rules can all diverge.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Reporting under more than one standard means preparing financial statements or reconciliations under two or more accounting frameworks, such as IFRS and US GAAP, or local statutory rules and a group standard. It covers primary statements, notes, segment disclosures, and the reconciliation schedules that explain why profit, equity, or cash flow differ between frameworks. The work sits with group finance, technical accounting, and external reporting teams, and it often involves auditors and regulators in each jurisdiction. The scope is not just translation of numbers, because recognition, measurement, presentation, and disclosure rules can all diverge.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The infrastructure is usually a consolidation or reporting system that holds multiple ledgers, a chart of accounts mapped to each framework, and a controlled set of adjustments. It may include ERP ledgers, a consolidation tool, a disclosure management platform, and spreadsheets for the last mile. Data must be tagged so the same transaction can carry different values under each standard without losing the audit trail. Version control, close calendars, and entity hierarchies are part of the same platform.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Teams start from a single source ledger or trial balance, then apply a framework specific adjustment layer for each standard. They document each difference with a policy reference, a calculation, and supporting evidence, then produce the statements and the reconciliation between them. Reviewers check that the adjustments are complete, consistent, and correctly classified, and that intercompany and consolidation effects are handled in the right order. Automation can help with mapping, tie outs, and disclosure drafting, but the technical accounting judgement stays with qualified people.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Each framework has its own authority, so the provenance of every adjustment matters, including the standard, interpretation, and internal policy that supports it. Rights and risk include audit exposure, regulatory filing obligations, and the possibility that one framework's treatment is not acceptable in another jurisdiction. Access controls, sign offs, and retention rules typically show who changed what and why. Where AI tools are used, the source data, model version, and review evidence need to be traceable, and personal or sensitive data must be handled under the relevant privacy and securities rules.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: More companies are reporting under multiple standards as they list in more than one market, acquire foreign subsidiaries, or face new sustainability and tax disclosure rules. Standard setters continue to converge on some topics while diverging on others, so the reconciliation workload is unlikely to disappear. AI assisted mapping, anomaly detection, and disclosure drafting are becoming part of the close, with humans retaining responsibility for judgement and sign off. The direction is toward continuous, tagged, and auditable multiple standard reporting rather than a once a year spreadsheet exercise.
